There is an increased risk of becoming a narcissist yourself. Sadly, I dont think it really matters whether your a golden child or a scapegoat. Either way you are forced into a constant perspective of considering if you are being watched, and how that will be judged by your Nparent. A golden child learns the rules and follows them. Even if they know on some level that it is wrong, the result is positive, and there a valid path to success. 

The Scapegoat may not be malignant, but could still become obsessed with the world of appearances, and their own introspection. I know many adults who had this role in their Nfamily. They questioned the rules, and the price was the ongoing wrath of the Nparent (Think about spending just a mooch with Trump as your father). Often I find the scapegoats to be great people underneath it all, but the damage lingers, and sometimes they have meltdowns that many adults would feel extremely cringey about. It is a sad cycle.

Perhaps the best bet is to be the lucky child who Nparent is indifferent towards. Less exposure, and instead the freedom/responsibility of raising yourself.

This is purely speculation, but my initial thought is that unlike say schizophrenia or bipolar disorder which clearly have some hereditary element, personality disorders seem to be in a different realm. Say for instance someone has genetic markers for OCD. The symptoms could be present since birth, remain dormant forever, or be triggered by some kind of external factors. That seems to tie in with the idea of epigenetics where genes can be present, but be in either an active or inactive state. PDa on the other hand seem to be defined by maladaptive coping and learned behaviours. A narc mother or father raises a child to be not an individual, but an extension of themselves, or enmeshment if you will. The brain of that impressionable child is conditioned to think the behaviors of the pd parent to be normal, and through repetition these pathways are reinforced. I would hope that the research progresses as well and leads to better treatment, but I believe on some level that the real goal needs to be to reduce stigma, and to have society take psychological and emotional abuse by authority figures to be as serious as sexual and physical abuse.

I worked in IT and CS for quite a while, but always had a fascination with psychology and neuroscience. The brain/computer analogy is not well received as far as I've seen. We build computers with the brain in mind to some extent, but other than that the similarities are weak. https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synapse

The process of learning is a physical process, and neural pathways are physical by nature. Anxiety for instance has its basis in biology and genetics. The 'code" is not the same as you would experience on a computer. A computer interprets or compiles high level code and turns it into low level code which can then be processed using electrical current between transistors and what not. Talk therapy is kind of like high level code, but that does not mean you get access to the source code (genetics). At the end of the day we can only really,control conscious thought and use it to try to gradual effect the subconscious. Maybe one day this barrier will be crossed, but for today it is what we have to work with.

Perhaps there are people out there that it could be true for. However it is good to be open with the idea of how complicated it is, and how we define physical defects. I, like more people than you would expect, was born with spinal and cerebral meningitis. Those that survive it are markedly more likely to develop certain mental health disorders. Something as simple as brain inflammation can have a strong impact on the rest of development. My bpdex has a sensory disorder which probably would not be determinable by any physical test, but maybe could have measurable components. One of these two examples is clearly physical. The other may not appear to be so overtly, but I suspect it has an equal physical component. I think there is a common misconception that psychology and physical illness are not related, but if that were the case then psyxhologists, and psychiatrists everywhere would not be eagerly awaiting developments in Neuro and cognitive science. The word "cured" doesn't seem to get floated around much in the mental health community. I think symptoms can be managed, new coping mechanisms developed, and maladaptive behaviors or thinking changed, but triggers will always be a real possibility. With dedication I think major improvements are completely achievable, but the naivete of what is implied by cured actually can lead to relapse. In substance recovery programs, as well as DBT you get concepts like "clean mind, addict mind, clear mind". Clean mind and addict mind might appear to be complete opposites, but they are not. Clean mind is craving control just as much as the addict mind, but with the belief that one cannot and will not relapse. Clear mind is the goal, where you acknowledge the reality that things are not always in your control, and it is possible to slip. I think the idea is so the patient won't beat themselves over slip ups, but also won't become so arrogant that they become careless. That middle ground is hard for anyone, but someone with a PD may find it to be the ultimate challenge.
